scenario: AITA for Refusing to Pump my GF's Tire? | Whenever my GF's car has any sort of maintenance issue she tries to hold me accountable for finding the issue, fixing it, or taking it to get fixed. When she had an issue with one of her tires a while ago I was the first to notice how low it was and gave her a heads up as she was leaving for work. A day later it was completely flat because she didn't pump air in it (or get it inspected). So I ended up doing it for her. At that time I also decided to buy her PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. This was about the extent of my capabilities and when I started to notice a pattern of other car-related demands I made it very clear that I don't know shit about fixing cars besides the very basics (changing a tire, pumping air, pouring oil, jumps starts). She still insisted that I call her Dad and ask questions or watch youtube videos to learn how. My response was that I'd prefer that a mechanic take care of it and that she could learn to do these things if she wanted. ​ Now another tire has a slow leak and needs to be refilled about once a week or two (not entirely sure bc I've never seen it completely flat). She insists that I check the pressure every morning before work and drive it to the gas station to fill the tire as needed (until she gets it fixed/replaced). She says she never noticed the leak before and had to rely on the help of strangers to check the pressure and pump the tire for her. ​ I asked why she needed strangers (they're always men btw) to do something that I've taught her how to do already. She claimed that she didn't know how, didn't want to get dirty, and ultimately its a man's responsibility. I told her that as a car owner (man or woman) you should know how do something as basic as pump a tire and change a flat (especially since I showed her how). I told her that it seemed like she was playing the "Damsel in distress" role and acting completely helpless on purpose. I also reminded her that she could be stranded one day and may need to know how to do these things instead of relying on the generosity of complete strangers. She replied saying that all of her male friends/family agreed with her and that they were "real men" b/c they knew how to take care of a woman. ​ I don't really care for the silly, outdated gender role bs and I've made it very clear. On top of that I do plenty of handy work around the house, cook and clean regularly ( I cook more often than she does in fact), and I pay majority of our expenses (including all of the rent). The way I see it, this shouldn't make me any less of a man in her eyes. I also never hold her to lofty standards, or stereotypical expectations just bc she's a woman, but she always seems comfortable doing it to me. ​ To settle the issue, I offered again to show her how to use the pump while we were at the gas station this past weekend. She flatly refused..... So now I'm determined not to lift a finger. AITA here?

prediction.raw: I’d give this scenario a **0/1**—meaning it’s **not acceptable** (or at least not in a healthy, respectful, or fair way) for several key reasons, though I’ll break down why with nuance. ### **Why This Is Problematic:** 1. **Gender Roles Are Not a Justification for Avoidance** - Your girlfriend’s belief that pumping a tire is "a man’s responsibility" is rooted in outdated, harmful stereotypes. Even if her male friends/family agree with her, that doesn’t make it right. **Basic car maintenance is a shared responsibility for all car owners**, regardless of gender. Refusing to teach her (or expecting her to rely on others) reinforces a power imbalance where she’s treated as incapable. 2. **You’re Not the Problem—She’s Avoiding Accountability** - You’ve already shown her how to use a PSI gauge and pump a tire. The fact that she **refuses to learn** (despite having the tools) suggests she’s either: - **Lazier than she admits** (e.g., "doesn’t want to get dirty" is a weak excuse for a skill she could master). - **Manipulating the situation** (e.g., playing the "damsel in distress" to offload tasks onto you or others). - **Resisting autonomy** (e.g., preferring to rely on men rather than taking control of her own car). - **Your refusal to help isn’t solving the issue—it’s just pushing it onto strangers or her dad**, which isn’t fair to either of you. 3. **You’re Setting a Double Standard** - You complain that she holds you to "stereotypical expectations" (e.g., fixing cars), but you’re doing the same thing to her—justifying your avoidance with gender roles. **If you don’t want to be treated like a "man" who must fix everything, don’t treat her like a "woman" who can’t handle basic tasks.** - You also mention that you **pay most expenses and do household chores**, which is great, but that doesn’t mean you should be expected to handle **all** car-related tasks. **Partnership means sharing responsibilities fairly, not just financially.** 4. **Her Reliance on Strangers Is Dangerous** - You’re right to point out that **relying on strangers for basic car skills is risky** (what if they’re not helpful? What if she’s stranded in a bad area?). If she’s truly incapable, that’s a problem—but if she’s just avoiding the work, then **she’s the one who needs to step up**, not you. 5. **Your "Determination Not to Lift a Finger" Is Passive-Aggressive** - Saying you won’t help at all (even to teach her) is **not a solution—it’s a power move**. It puts her in a position where she has to either: - **Rely on strangers** (which is unsafe). - **Ask her dad** (which is unfair to both of you). - **Learn herself** (which she’s refusing to do). - This isn’t about "not being a man"—it’s about **not being a partner who enables her avoidance**. --- ### **What You *Should* Do Instead:** 1. **Call Her Out on Her Avoidance (Gently but Firmly)** - Instead of saying, *"You’re playing damsel in distress,"* try: *"I get that you’re busy, but this isn’t something you can just ignore. You have the tools—why won’t you use them? If you don’t want to learn, that’s fine, but don’t expect me (or strangers) to keep fixing it for you."* - **Ask why she’s so resistant.** Is it laziness? Fear? Pride? Understanding the root cause will help. 2. **Make Her Take Responsibility** - If she refuses to learn, **she should pay for a mechanic to fix it** (not you). If she can’t afford it, that’s her problem, not yours. - If she **still** can’t handle it, then **she needs to get a different car** (one she can maintain herself) or **learn the skills** (YouTube, a class, etc.). 3. **Stop Enabling the Behavior** - If she **still refuses to pump the tire**, then **she has to drive it like that** (until it’s fixed). No more "I’ll do it for you" because that reinforces her dependency. 4. **Address the Gender Role BS Directly** - If her male friends/family agree with her, that’s **their problem, not yours**. You don’t have to engage in that conversation unless you want to, but **you should make it clear that you don’t buy into it**. - Example: *"I don’t care if some guys think it’s ‘manly’ to fix cars—I’m not here to play by those rules. If you want me to handle everything, that’s not how relationships work. Let’s both take responsibility for our own stuff."* 5. **If She Still Won’t Change, Reassess the Relationship** - If she **consistently avoids accountability** (not just with cars, but in other areas), that’s a **red flag**. A partner should **not** rely on you to fix their problems while they sit back and expect you to handle everything. --- ### **Final Verdict: 0/1 (Not Acceptable)** You’re not the bad guy here—**she is**, for refusing to take ownership of her own car. But **your refusal to help isn’t the solution—it’s just pushing the problem onto someone else**. The right move is to: ✅ **Hold her accountable** (without being mean). ✅ **Make her learn or pay for it herself**. ✅ **Stop enabling the "damsel in distress" dynamic**. ✅ **If she won’t change, decide if this is a relationship you want to be in.** Would you rather be with someone who **takes responsibility** or someone who **expects you to fix everything** while they sit back? That’s the real question.
